A hedgehog ballooned up like a Christmas pudding because of trapped wind – but is now on the road to recovery after being ‘popped’ by a vet.
The prickly patient named Penelope tripled in size due to a rare condition called ‘balloon syndrome’ where gas, usually caused by bacterial infection after an injury, gets trapped under the skin.
Without immediate treatment hedgehogs can go into shock from it and die.
Penelope was taken into Apex Vets in Denny, Stirlingshire, after being found by a concerned member of the public on November 16.
An x-ray showed she had become huge, swelling from her usual 4cm or 1.6in diameter to a whopping 13cm – 5.1in.
Concerned vets ‘popped’ her, draining a whopping 600ml of air to relieve the pressure, as she kept reinflating to the size of a small football.

title: Australian worker wins A$17,861 after employer fails to consider vacant role before AI-linked redundancy
summary: An Australian contracts administrator faced dismissal as the employer attributed this to the reduced necessity for his role due to AI tools. text:
An Australian worker earning A$155,000 a year has won an unfair dismissal case after his employer partly blamed artificial intelligence tools for making his position unnecessary. The Fair Work Commission found that the company no longer needed his job, but ruled that his dismissal was unfair because he could reasonably have been moved into another vacant position. Commissioner McKinnon ordered LVL80 SLR Pty Ltd to pay the former employee A$17,861.54 in compensation. Of this amount, A$12,115.39 must be paid directly to the worker, while A$5,746.15 must go into his superannuation account. The decision was known as Basic v LVL80 SLR Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4327 and was delivered in Sydney earlier this month on 6 November. It shows an important point for employers: even when a job is genuinely no longer needed, they must consider whether an affected employee could reasonably move into another available role before ending their employment.

The Supreme Court of Canada on Friday upheld Quebec's highly contested 2019 law that bans religious symbols in the public sector.
It was, more than anything, seen to be targeting Muslim women in the province who wear the hijab, but also impacted Catholics, Sikhs and other minorities.
Quebec's population is 5 percent Muslim, according to the last census carried out in 2021. That figure is second only to Ontario.
Amira Elghawaby, who was Canada’s first and only special representative on combatting Islamophobia, until her office was shut down earlier this year, called the verdict "devastating".
"The promise of Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms has been broken, and could be broken again and again. She had moved back in with her mum and her son's father was no longer in the picture.
"I was at this point where I was depressed and suicidal," she says.
At 35 weeks, she suffered reduced fetal movement and bleeding, leading to her pregnancy being labelled high-risk.
"It got to the point where I was so paranoid that my baby was actually dead inside me, or dying," she says.

text:
BERLIN, November 27. /TASS/. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is calling for the closure of Germany's borders to Ukrainian refugees, asserting that "Germany should not bear responsibility for the entire world." This assertion was made by Markus Frohnmaier, the deputy leader and foreign policy spokesman for the AfD faction in the Bundestag.
"We will close our borders. I am a German politician. Addressing the issues in Ukraine is not my responsibility," Frohnmaier declared in remarks published by the newspaper Bild. He further emphasized that the party aims to repatriate all Ukrainians currently residing in Germany, claiming that such a move would help secure "safe borders" for the country.

summary: The Jigawa State Independent Electoral Commission (JISIEC) Chairman, Auwalu Harbo said the proposed 2 October 2027 date aligns with constitutional provisions and the Electoral Act 2026, which requires at least 300 days' notice before an election. The post Jigawa announces 2 October 2027 date for local government elections appeared first on Premium Times Nigeria .
text:
The Jigawa State Independent Electoral Commission (JISIEC) has proposed 2 October 2027, for the next local government councils’ elections.
The commission’s Chairman, Auwalu Harbo, announced this on Thursday at a stakeholders’ engagement meeting in Dutse.
Mr Harbo said the proposed date aligns with constitutional provisions and the Electoral Act 2026, which requires at least 300 days’ notice before an election.

A preserved two-bedroom house designed by architect John Lautner in 1947 has been listed for sale in the Hollywood Hills for $2,850,000. Known as the Florence Polin House, it measures 1,342 square feet and stands at 3542 Multiview Drive, above the Cahuenga Pass. It sits on a hillside plot covering more than half an acre. One of the home's most unusual features is the way its roof is supported. A three-point steel truss carries the weight, so the inside walls do not need to support the roof. According to LA Digs, the property is listed by Mortimer Canepa of Berkshire Hathaway and Nicole Kornhauser of Carolwood Estates. Our Arabic word of the week, khayma, meaning tent, stems from the three-letter root kha, ya and meem. Its plural forms include khiyam and khaymat.
The verb khayyama means to pitch a tent or set up camp. Takhyeem refers to the activity of camping, while mukhayyam means camp, whether established for recreational, educational or humanitarian purposes.
The verb also has figurative applications, describing something that has descended on or enveloped a place. Khayyama al samt means silence has fallen, while khayyama al huzn describes an atmosphere overcome by sadness.
Another derivative is khayyam, meaning tentmaker. Perhaps the most famous bearer of the name is Omar Khayyam, the 11th-century mathematician, astronomer and poet. His surname is believed to have originated from his family's profession.

title: Justice delayed: why the Rohingya verdict may change little on the ground
text:
There were cheers, tears and prayers across the world’s largest refugee settlement in Cox’s Bazar when the International Court of Justice pronounced Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya. Who can grudge their moment after what they have endured?
It is a bitter-sweet moment, nevertheless. To have the wrongs against them acknowledged reaffirms their basic humanity. However, alongside comes the stigma of victimhood, as with other recognised genocide victims such as European Jews, Rwandan Tutsi, Bosnian Muslims, Sudanese Darfuris and Iraqi Yazidis.
The recovery path from genocide is long, fraught and uncertain. How successfully that is traversed depends not on formal judicial announcements but what they change. That is what the Rohingya ask as celebrations fade, and lawyers and campaigners move beyond self-congratulations.

WASHINGTON - An international team of marine geologists using a remotely operated submarine in an abyss in the western Pacific Ocean has found evidence of the deepest-known explosive volcanic eruption on Earth as much as 6,500m below the surface.
The researchers sailed to the Mariana Trench, among the deepest oceanic valleys on the planet, to deploy a remotely operated vehicle, or ROV, called Jason/Medea. They used the ROV to study the trench walls around the deepest-known point of seabed on Earth, called the Challenger Deep.
The ROV observed and collected pyroclastic rocks, telltale evidence of an explosive volcanic eruption composed of ejected rock fragments and volcanic glass.

The Taliban is continuing its crackdown on women's rights in Afghanistan by stripping women of their names and replacing them with 'granny' or 'goat.'
A joint investigation by Zan News and The Guardian found that healthcare workers in the Balkh province have been instructed to refer to women as 'bibi,' meaning 'granny.'
Officials said this instruction must be observed even on medical prescriptions.
Lalah Osmany, an Afghan activist living in Germany, told El Pais that the Taliban are also referring to women as 'goats' and 'cows.'
Other times, she says women are presented in official documents as the 'wife' or 'daughter' of a male relative.

Israeli drone strike on vehicle kills Palestinian man in northern Gaza
A Palestinian man was killed and several others were wounded on Friday evening in an Israeli drone strike on a vehicle in the northern Gaza Strip, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
The strike hit the vehicle in the Bir al-Naaja area, west of the Jabalia refugee camp, killing Khaled Assaf, witnesses told Wafa.
Some of the wounded were in serious condition.
Separately, a child was wounded by Israeli gunfire in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip.
Israeli forces stationed near the area's eastern perimeter repeatedly opened fire towards tents sheltering displaced Palestinians, wounding the child.
The Palestinian health ministry said on Thursday that Israeli attacks had killed at least 19 Palestinians and wounded 48 others over the past 48 hours.
The latest attacks brought the total number of Palestinians killed since the so-called ceasefire began in October last year to 1,705.

text:
The Anambra State Government has postponed its statewide end-of-year environmental sanitation exercise scheduled for Saturday, November 28, to December 5, 2026, to allow residents participate in the Independent National Electoral Commission’s mock accreditation exercise.
The state Commissioner for Environment, Clem Aguiyi, announced the change in a public notice issued by the Ministry of Environment on Friday.
He said the postponement was necessary to avoid disrupting INEC’s nationwide mock accreditation and result upload exercise, which is scheduled to begin at 8:30am on Saturday.

It was not their first face-to-face encounter, they have long crossed paths at the UN, APEC and the G20, and their diplomats have negotiated jointly on North Korea and Iran, but it marks an important moment in great-power diplomacy.
What was billed as Yalta 2.0, in reference to the 1945 conference in Crimea where Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin divided up spheres of influence in the postwar order, was nothing of this sort. This was not a meeting of three victors of a great war, but of three major powers seeking to set the rules of their relationship in a changing world, at a time when U.S. global hegemony is being questioned.

At least eight found dead on migrant boat off Spain's Canary Islands
MADRID, Nov 27 - At least eight migrants were found dead when a boat carrying about 100 people was rescued near Spain's Canary Islands, the maritime rescue service said on Friday, as a surge in arrivals overwhelms authorities in the region.
The deaths highlight the dangers of one of the world's deadliest migration routes just days before Sunday's general election in Spain, where immigration has emerged as a defining campaign issue.
Between 8 and 10 bodies were found on board and 6 people were airlifted to a hospital in serious condition, the rescue service said. The boat, discovered 39 nautical miles (72 km) south of the island of El Hierro, was being towed to the port of La Estaca.
Eighty-four survivors disembarked from a separate boat at the island's La Restinga port, home to a migrant reception centre and field hospital where most migrant boats reaching the island have been processed.

A man in Sweden had his penis, prostate and bladder removed after being misdiagnosed with the wrong form of cancer.
The unnamed patient was diagnosed with prostate cancer at Skaraborg Hospital in Skövde in 2023.
A pathologist at diagnostic services provider Unilabs analysed the man's tissue samples, which were interpreted as indicating that he had prostate cancer, according to Swedish news outlet Bulletin.
However, seven months later, further tests revealed that the man was suffering from squamous cell carcinoma - a malignant tumour that forms on the surface of the skin.
According to Unilabs, the incorrect diagnosis meant that the cancer had continued to grow, and so surgeons were forced to amputate his penis and also made the decision to remove his prostate and bladder.
The removal of the man's organs means his urine and faeces are now diverted through openings in his abdomen.

Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.
The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.
Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.
The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.

title: Russia Expects Oil Production of 494 Mmt in 2026
summary: Russia Expects Oil Production of 494 Mmt in 2026 Egypt Oil & Gas
text:
Russia expects to produce approximately 494 million metric tons (mmt) of oil in 2026, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on November 27, according to state news agency TASS.
The estimate is lower than the Economic Development Ministry’s projections in both its baseline and conservative scenarios.
The ministry forecasts oil and condensate production of 511 mmt in 2026 under its baseline scenario, virtually unchanged from 511.4 mmt in 2025.
Under this scenario, production is expected to increase to 516 mmt in 2027 and 525 mmt annually in 2028 and 2029.
Under the conservative scenario, the ministry projects a 2.8% decline in output in 2026 to 497.2 mmt, followed by a gradual recovery to 502.2 mmt in 2027, 507.2 mmt in 2028, and 512.2 mmt in 2029.

title: Russia has lost at least 87 members of its most secretive special forces unit since invading Ukraine, investigation finds
summary: At least 87 members of Russia’s Special Operations Forces (SSO) have died since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, iStories, an independent Russian investigative outlet, found after examining a leaked Rosstat database of death records.
text:
At least 87 members of Russia’s Special Operations Forces (SSO) have died since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, iStories, an independent Russian investigative outlet, found after examining a leaked Rosstat database of death records.
Rosstat data show that at least 54 SSO operatives died in Ukraine and three died of wounds in Russian hospitals. Five died in Syria, and five more are believed to have been killed in sabotage operations Ukrainian security services carried out in Russia. The remaining deaths were not linked to combat or occurred under unclear circumstances.
The Special Operations Forces is considered the most secretive combat unit in the Russian military. It draws its best operatives from elite special forces units of Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, and its total strength is estimated at between 2,500 and 7,000 troops, depending on the source.

summary: Quebec’s ban on teachers and police wearing religious symbols such as hijabs and turbans on the job remains in place.
text:
Canada’s top court largely upholds Quebec’s religious symbols ban
Quebec’s ban on teachers and police wearing religious symbols such as hijabs and turbans at work remains in place.
A landmark ruling by Canada’s Supreme Court has largely upheld Quebec’s secularism law, leaving in place a ban on public school teachers, police officers and some other public employees wearing religious symbols at work.
The court ruled on Friday that requiring elected members of Quebec’s National Assembly to uncover their faces infringes upon their democratic rights. That part of the law cannot be enforced against them.
The court also weighed in on a question that goes beyond Quebec — how far governments can go in using the notwithstanding clause.

title: Saudi Arabia shoots down 90 per cent of Houthi missiles in five-month barrage
text:
Saudi Arabia has intercepted nine out of every 10 missiles and drones launched against it during five months of sustained attacks mainly by Houthi rebels, an intelligence assessment passed to The National has revealed.
The kingdom’s air defence network, which includes Patriot and Thaad interceptors, destroyed 252 of at least 278 hostile munitions fired from Yemen and Iraq that were registered between June 27 and November 27.
The report by Project Aurorah, a Middle East intelligence and surveillance platform, also highlighted the continuing danger to civilians and critical infrastructure from the missiles that get through.
Of 43 recorded ground impacts, 17 were caused by debris from missiles or drones intercepted by Saudi forces. The remaining 26 were direct impacts by hostile munitions, representing just over 9 per cent of the total incoming threat.

text:
The Russian government announced Friday that it will extend its ban on jet fuel exports until the end of March 2027 as the domestic energy market continues to feel the strain from Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries.
Russia first banned jet fuel exports in June following Ukrainian drone attacks on refineries that led to slumps in domestic production and localized shortages. That embargo was set to expire on Monday, Nov. 30.

If you’re reading this, then your media feed, like mine, is probably full of cats.
That’s hardly surprising. The internet has always belonged to cats, which suits me just fine: I love cats and live with four of them.
But in one of the classes I’ve taught, Cats: Why We Love Them, I explain how our affection for the house cat, Felis silvestris catus, is a relatively recent phenomenon in the scope of human history. In many parts of the world, cats were viewed with suspicion and subjected to terrible mistreatment.

title: Arsenic in the water: Thailand presses Myanmar over mining pollution
summary: Thailand is seeking to tackle river pollution stemming from rare-earth mines in neighboring Myanmar. The two countries held joint talks this week as a "first step towards agreeing on the evidence."
text:
Thailand presses Myanmar over mining pollution
November 27, 2026
Thailand is pushing its neighbor Myanmar to take on unregulated mining.
A toxic border river is putting lives and livelihoods at risk in northern Thailand. The Kok River, once rich in fish, is now polluted with arsenic, mercury, and other hazardous contaminants.
The reason is the mining activity in the militia-controlled regions of Myanmar. Most of these mines are located in Shan state, where civil war has raged since the 2021 military coup.
The mining activity is driven in part by China's dominant rare earth industry.
Two sides agreed to joint water sampling
Bangkok this week hosted the first Thai-Myanmar working group where it said tests proved rare-earth and gold mines in Myanmar were the reason of the pollution downstream. China was also present in the talks.

The attack damaged transmission equipment in the city of Rovenki. Television broadcasts are completely unavailable there, while radio services are partially disrupted in the city and Sverdlovsk municipal district, as well as parts of Antratsit and Krasnodon districts and nearby settlements.
Six radio stations continue broadcasting despite the damage: Respublika FM, Pobeda, Vremya FM, Radio Russia, Mayak and Svoya Volna.

Still, he keeps writing.
"Fear is one of the main motivations for my writing, particularly fear associated with war," he told AFP in an interview during a short trip to Khartoum, where he attended a literary event.

UK government deleted record of meeting between Blair and Shabana Mahmood
The British government deleted the record of a meeting between former prime minister Tony Blair and Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, according to the Democracy for Sale newsletter.
The meeting, which took place in June 2025 when Mahmood was justice secretary, was originally declared as official government business, with its purpose listed as "stakeholder engagement".
But when we asked for details of what was discussed under the Freedom of Information Act, the Ministry of Justice told Democracy for Sale it was a "party-political" meeting and that no records of it existed.
Several days after the newsletter asked the government for comment, the meeting disappeared from the public register.
Blair is a member of US President Donald Trump's Gaza "Board of Peace", while Mahmood has pushed for increasingly draconian legislation on migration and maintained the government's ban on Palestine Action.

title: AI debt boom could push up funding costs for South Africa
summary: Tech giants are tapping global debt markets to borrow hundreds of billions of dollars at the same time as governments.
text:
South Africaâs central bank warned that heavy borrowing by Western technology companies developing artificial intelligence could push up funding costs just as Pretoria approaches a refinancing crunch.
Tech giants are tapping global debt markets to borrow hundreds of billions of dollars at the same time as governments, creating competition for long-term capital that could make it more expensive for South Africa, the bank said. The Bank of England said hyperscaler bond sales were set to exceed $300 billion in 2026, or roughly 8% of global investment-grade issuance.
The warning comes as South Africa prepares to enter one of its heaviest refinancing periods, with maturing debt expected to more than double to roughly $23 billion annually between 2030 and 2032. The South African Reserve Bank also warned that a drop in AI shares could push up yields and weaken the rand because South African savers hold 13% of their assets in AI-related equities.

With a quick flick of the wrist, Umaru Zayyanu conveys the phrase “I am a Nigerian”.

text:
Budget carrier Norse Atlantic filed for bankruptcy Friday, saying it failed to secure funding after soaring fuel costs strained the company's operations throughout the year.
Its parent company, Norse Atlantic ASA, concluded that the Norwegian carrier no longer has a basis to continue operations.
"Despite extensive efforts, the Company has so far not been able to secure sufficient funding to meet its short-term liquidity needs," the firm said in a statement Friday.
It comes days after Norse said it's facing a "critical financial situation" and was considering its options from a strategic takeover to ACMI contracts, which refer to short-term capacity leasing. The company's shares closed 85% lower on Wednesday.
The board has now filed a bankruptcy petition with the Agder District Court, where a trustee will be appointed to manage the process further.

KARACHI: The death toll from the collapse of an under-construction six-storey building near Karachi’s Baloch Colony area rose to eight on Friday after rescue workers recovered four more bodies from the rubble.
On Wednesday, three people were killed and 14 others injured when an under-construction building — reportedly being constructed illegally on a residential plot — collapsed. Another body was recovered on Thursday, taking the death toll to four.
On Friday, a Rescue 1122 spokesperson said the total number of bodies recovered from the rubble had reached eight.

MOSCOW, November 27. /TASS/. The net profit of the Russian Railways holding under International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) for January-September 2026 totaled 86.2 bln rubles ($1.5 bln) and soared by nearly four times in annual terms, the company said.
Total revenue of Russian Railways for the reporting period increased by 18.5% to 3.2 trillion rubles ($39 bln).
The holding's operating expenses amounted to 2.6 trillion rubles ($31.7 bln), and operating profit stood at 584.6 bln rubles ($7.1 bln). EBITDA for the first nine months of 2026 reached 1 trillion rubles ($12.2 bln).
The holding also reported that revenue from freight transportation and infrastructure access totaled 2.1 trillion rubles ($25.6 bln), while revenue from passenger transportation came to 413 bln rubles ($5 bln).

ISLAMABAD: Short-term inflation was recorded at 9.49 per cent year-on-year in the week ending on Nov 26, driven largely by wheat flour prices, according to official data released by the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS) on Friday.
The index comprises 51 items, with prices collected from 50 markets in 17 cities, and is calculated weekly to track changes in the prices of essential commodities and services.
The data showed that the prices of 20 commodities increased, while those of nine items declined. Meanwhile, the prices of 22 items remained unchanged from the previous week.
Short-term inflation has entered single digits after several weeks owing to a decline in petroleum products prices. It had remained in the double digits for several consecutive weeks, largely due to persistently elevated petrol and diesel prices.

title: The Gambia election: Can Barrow secure a third term?
summary: President Adama Barrow is seeking a third term as Gambians vote on December 5. The election will test the opposition's appeal and the country's progress on democratic reform.
text:
The Gambia election: Can Barrow secure a third term?
November 27, 2026
The Gambia votes on December 5 in a presidential election that takes place nearly 10 years after voters ended Yahya Jammeh's 22-year rule.
President Adama Barrow, who succeeded Jammeh in 2017, is running for a third term despite an earlier pledge not to do so.
Barrow is running against the tiny West African country's main opposition leader Ousainou Darboe of the United Democratic Party, youth candidate Talib Ahmed Bensouda, who until last week was mayor of Kanifing Municipality, and five other candidates.
The field also includes independent candidates Almameh Gibba, a lawmaker who is backed by Jammeh, and former Vice President Isatou Touray, the only female in the presidential race.
What matters to voters
The Gambia is still governed under its 1997 Constitution, which was adopted during Jammeh's rule.
A proposed replacement, which included presidential term limits, was rejected by the National Assembly in July 2025

summary: The November sell-off has so far pushed the S&P 500 into a correction. History shows that a correction doesn't always lead to a bear market, or a recession.
text:
The S&P 500 fell into a correction on Nov. 20 for the first time since April 2025 as stocks pulled back sharply from October's record highs.
The market correction, defined as a 10% decline from a recent high, came as investor concern mounted over a potential slowdown in AI spending, mega-cap tech valuations and the path of Federal Reserve interest rate policy. The S&P 500 fell 3.7% on Nov. 20 alone, closing at 6,910.39, its seventh consecutive daily decline. That left the index 11.6% below the Oct. 6 closing high of 7,818.93.

text:
A French court of appeal has ordered the seizure of €37 million ($40 million) in assets belonging to Riad Salameh as he faces the prospect of a trial in France for embezzlement of Lebanese public funds.

title: Risks of child marriage in Iran complicated by war
summary: War, poverty and disrupted schooling could put more girls in Iran at risk of child marriage, rights advocates warn.
text:
Risks of child marriage in Iran complicated by war
November 27, 2026
For a girl still at school, marriage can mean leaving her education behind, becoming pregnant before adulthood and growing dependent on her family and husband.
In Iran, rights advocates warn that war and mounting financial hardship could expose more girls to those risks.
The warning comes as the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage is observed on November 27. The day was established during the UN General Assembly last year.
Although there is no evidence linking child marriages to the war, cases illustrate the danger faced by girls married as children, often with limited means of escaping abuse. Gaps in Iran's marriage statistics also make it difficult to measure the conflict's impact.
In one case cited by the Iranian human rights news agency HRANA, a 14-year-old girl in Kerman province who had recently given birth was reportedly killed by her husband.

World AIDS Day 2026 is my last as Executive Director of UNAIDS. Today, we remember the nearly 45 million people we have lost to AIDS and we stand in solidarity with the 41 million people living with HIV and with the communities who have carried this response forward with courage, determination and love.

Pride in what has been achieved through science, solidarity and struggle. Concern that, at the very moment when we have the tools to end AIDS, political choices and deepening inequalities threaten to put that goal beyond our reach.

These trends have come alongside a corresponding rise in attempts to explain this phenomenon, ranging from feckless leadership and rising inequality to globalization and economic shocks. While those are all factors, a more compelling explanation could lie in how the digital revolution has undermined trust in facts, governments, and democracy itself.

text:

title: Russia’s oil production to reach around 494 mln metric tons in 2026 — Novak
summary: Under the baseline scenario, Russian Economic Development Ministry expects production to increase to 516 mln metric tons in 2027
text:
ISTANBUL, November 27. /TASS/. Russia plans to produce 494 mln metric tons of oil this year, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters.
"According to the Energy Ministry’s data, around 494 mln [metric tons]," he said.
According to the Economic Development Ministry’s forecast for Russia’s socioeconomic development for 2027 and the 2028-2029 planning period, Russia’s oil production, including condensate, will remain virtually unchanged from 2025 levels under the baseline scenario, totaling 511 mln metric tons in 2026 compared with 511.4 mln metric tons a year earlier.
Under the baseline scenario, the ministry expects production to increase to 516 mln metric tons in 2027 and reach 525 mln metric tons in both 2028 and 2029.
The conservative scenario envisages a 2.8% decline in production this year to 497.2 mln metric tons, followed by an increase to 502.2 mln metric tons in 2027, 507.2 mln metric tons in 2028, and 512.2 mln metric tons in 2029.

title: WWII veteran receives Purple Heart at 99, 81 years after 1945 injury
text:
A 99-year-old US World War II veteran who was wounded by enemy shellfire in Germany in March 1945 has finally received his Purple Heart, 81 years after the incident. Glenn Fisher, who served with the 556th Anti-Aircraft Artillery Unit, was injured in an attack that killed two of his comrades, but never received the medal because of problems with his military records. After more than a year of efforts by his longtime friend Jeff Thoke to overcome the documentation hurdles, Fisher was presented with the award at a ceremony at the Frazier Kentucky History Museum on July 1, 2026.
Why did a World War II veteran wait 81 years for his Purple Heart
According to the Frazier Kentucky History Museum, Fisher was injured in March 1945 while serving with the 556th Anti-Aircraft Artillery Unit in Germany. Enemy shells struck and exploded, injuring 14 members of his unit. Two of his comrades were killed in the incident, including his close friend Paul Baker.

TEHRAN – Iran’s Maryam Abdollahpour claimed the silver medal at the World Para Taekwondo Grand Prix Final on Friday.
The Iranian representative in the women’s under-57kg category sustained an injury during her semifinal bout against a Chinese opponent at the Para Taekwondo Grand Prix underway in Astana, Kazakhstan.

summary: When East Germany could no longer afford to import coffee, it introduced a substitute blend containing rye and chicory in 1977. A public outcry ensued. The solution to the problem lay 9,000 kilometers away — in Vietnam.

November 27, 2026
Coffee lovers, brace yourselves: Imagine taking your first sip, expecting the rich aroma of roasted coffee beans, only to discover that your cup contains a concoction made from ingredients you can barely identify.
That's exactly what millions of outraged East Germans experienced in 1977. But what led to this?
Foreign currency deficit versus soaring prices
A poor harvest in Brazil saw global coffee prices skyrocketing, creating a major problem for East Germany. Unlike West Germany's Deutsche Mark, the East German Mark was a domestic currency with no value abroad.
Even under normal circumstances, the country constantly struggled to obtain the hard currency it needed to pay for imports. title: Anonymous California donors protect 120 acres of redwood forest for salmon
text:
Two anonymous landowners in California have made an unusual contribution to conservation by donating a conservation easement valued at more than $680,000 to permanently protect 120 acres of privately owned forest in the Santa Cruz Mountains. The property, located in the Upper Zayante River watershed near Felton, includes more than 67 acres of redwood forest, along with oak woodlands, Douglas fir trees and other diverse habitats. The donation was made to Sempervirens Fund, California's first land trust, in December 2023 and announced publicly on January 4, 2024. The agreement restricts future development, subdivision and commercial timber harvesting while allowing the owners to continue enjoying the property for low-impact recreational activities. The protected landscape also plays an important role in safeguarding waterways connected to endangered coho salmon habitat.

title: Why Must the Suez Canal Stay Open to Ships of Every Nation?
summary: Why Must the Suez Canal Stay Open to Ships of Every Nation? Diplomacy and Law
text:
Why Must the Suez Canal Stay Open to Ships of Every Nation?
Introduction
The Suez Canal belongs to Egypt, but international law prevents the Egyptian government from arbitrarily excluding foreign vessels. Article I of the 1888 Convention of Constantinople guarantees passage to commercial ships and warships without discrimination based on their flag, during both peace and war, subject to applicable legal restrictions.
Connecting the Mediterranean Sea with the Red Sea, the canal provides a direct maritime route between Europe and Asia, allowing vessels to avoid circumnavigating southern Africa. Its geographical position makes uninterrupted navigation particularly important for international commerce, energy transportation, and naval movements.
Egypt retains sovereignty over the waterway, including the authority to regulate navigation, collect transit fees, and protect national security. International law, however, establishes limits on the circumstances in which Egypt may exercise these

Witnesses told police the elephant appeared to be unharmed and retreated back into the jungle.

title: Indian workers fill Germany's labor gaps but face hurdles and risks
summary: The number of Indians working in Germany has grown rapidly in recent years. But many continue to face challenges in the labor market. Some also fall victim to recruitment scams, leaving them vulnerable to exploitation.
text:
Indian workers fill Germany's labor gaps but face hurdles and risks
November 27, 2026
Pratyay Saikia was studying food technology in 2022 when he saw an advertisement from Magic Billion, a recruitment agency that places skilled and semi-skilled Indian professionals in verified jobs abroad.
The 25-year-old from the northern Indian state of Haryana reached out to explore employment opportunities.
Four years later, he is working as a butcher at Metzgerei Lederer in southern Germany, having completed a three-year apprenticeship at the butcher shop.
"I came to Baden-Württemberg with 180 other Indians who came here to do an Ausbildung [apprenticeship] program. Me and seven others did our Ausbildung at Lederer [butcher shop], while others went into the construction sector. I now have a full-time job here," Saikia told DW.
He is not alone as the number of Indian workers subject to social security contributions in Germany has grown sevenfold over the past decade, to over 140,000 professionals.

text:
ISTANBUL, November 27. /TASS/. Gazprom and Turkey’s Botas have signed a contract extending gas supplies to the country for three years on the same terms, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters on the sidelines of the Russian-Turkish business forum.

title: Russia Bans Buckwheat Exports Until Mid-2027
summary: The government cited a declining harvest and shrinking stockpiles for introducing the export ban.
text:
The Russian government announced Friday that it will impose a six-month ban on buckwheat exports amid a declining harvest and shrinking stockpiles.
“The decision was made to maintain stability on the domestic food market,” the government said in a statement.
The ban goes into effect on Saturday and expires on May 28, 2027. Russia last imposed a temporary export ban on buckwheat in the summer of 2021.
The ban makes an exception for exports to member countries of the Moscow-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), the breakaway pro-Russia Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, as well as for humanitarian aid deliveries.

The record was registered between 18 and 24 November.

text:

Across 14 country operations, UNHCR’s 2025 GBV Impact Report found that 171 safe spaces supported by UNHCR and partners were shuttered last year, with further closures in 2026; 203 remained open. When safe spaces close, specialized services are cut, or referral pathways weakened, survivors have fewer opportunities to safely disclose abuse and seek help.

Nov 27 - Four Jehovah's Witnesses have been convicted of "extremist" activity in Russian-annexed Crimea and sentenced to up to eight years in prison, the faith group said, among the longest terms handed to members since Moscow banned the movement in 2017.
Jarrod Lopes, a New York-based spokesperson for the Christian group, said the case, which concluded on Wednesday, had been based on secret witnesses and wiretaps of conversations between believers.
Defendants Alexander Kopylets, Alexander Voronchikhin and Dmitriy Zakharevich were sentenced respectively to 8, 7-1/2 and 6-1/2 years, while Yekaterina Demidova received a 3-year suspended sentence, he said.
Over the years, six other members have received eight-year sentences, so far the harshest punishment Russia has handed out linked to the group, he added.

text:
Let the Jankara moment pass. Let the market hear that Nigeria is serious. Now let the diplomats return to the quiet room, but this time, with South Africa fully aware that Nigeria’s patience is not infinite, and with Nigeria fully aware that its strength lies in disciplined follow-through, not in perpetual shouting.
Professor Babafemi Badejo’s article onJankara diplomacy is elegantly written, learned, and with respect mistimed.
It is right about the Vienna Convention. It is right that diplomacy is a conservative trade. It is right that an envoy must act “within the limits permitted by international law” under Article 3(1)(b).
Where it misses the point is on timing and context. For years, Nigeria has practised the quiet, correct, conservative diplomacy that Badejo prescribes in Pretoria. Ukraine's Unified Register of Persons Missing in Special Circumstances currently contains information on more than 117,000 people.

summary: AMSTERDAM, Nov 27 - Dutch authorities seized 26 critically endangered Vallarta mud turtles at Schiphol airport last week, the Dutch Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said on Friday.
text:
Dutch authorities seize critically endangered turtles at Schiphol airport
AMSTERDAM, Nov 27 - Dutch authorities seized 26 critically endangered Vallarta mud turtles at Schiphol airport last week, the Dutch Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said on Friday.
The Vallarta turtles, one of the world's smallest turtle species, were brought in from Mexico, where only around 300 of them remain in the wild.
They were hidden in the checked baggage of a man who was travelling to Hong Kong, the NVWA said. The man was arrested and further investigations are ongoing.
Wrapped in duct tape to prevent them from moving, most of the turtles were packed in a box together with a toy car, while a few others were placed inside a sealed sock.
NVWA said they all survived and were taken to a specialist animal rescue centre.
Vallarta mud turtles can sell for up to $30,000 each, the US-based Center for Biological Diversity said last month in a statement calling on the Mexican government to do more

Police in India say they have uncovered an international cyberfraud and human trafficking operation on the outskirts of capital city Delhi and rescued 92 Indonesian and 72 Malaysian nationals.
They were allegedly lured to India with promises of lucrative IT jobs, but forced into cyber crime, according to police.
Police say the scheme was exposed after a Malaysian worker managed to escape and revealed the operation.
Dozens of foreign nationals have alleged that once they arrived in India, their passports were confiscated and they were held against their will in Noida - a Delhi suburb that is a major IT and business hub in northern India and home to several call centres.

Can luxury save Macy's?

Leaving the Macy's flagship store in New York, the Niesig family visiting from Germany sizes up their loot: a pair of sweatpants for mom, a Hurley jacket for dad, Ugg boots for their daughter. Son Mika, 16, is the only one empty-handed.
"I like zipper hoodies, and there was one zipper from Levi's that was pretty cool," he says. "But in the end, I didn't buy it because it was just a little boring."

It's one of the biggest fears about getting older: losing your memory. A growing body of evidence shows we can do a lot to lower the risk of dementia, starting with changes to our day-to-day habits.
For decades, dementia was seen as something determined by genes or bad luck: a disease that strikes late in life with little anyone can do about it. That thinking has radically changed.
In 2024, the Lancet Commission, an international panel of experts, identified 14 modifiable risk factors for dementia and estimated that about 45% of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed. title: More than one million Americans from the South, Midwest and to the East Coast without power as Thanksgiving storm slams the US sparking holiday travel nightmare
summary: More than 2,400 flights were delayed and 459 were canceled on Thursday because of the historic foul weather. Further interruptions are expected Friday.
text:
More than one million Americans were left without power on Thanksgiving as a massive storm battered the country and caused severe travel disruptions.
The holiday storm saw powerful rain and strong gusts of wind hit the South, Midwest and East Coast throughout the day.
As of Thursday night, most of the power losses were in the east coast, where more than 610,000 customers had lost electricity in just Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Maryland and Virginia, according to Poweroutage.us.
In New Jersey, widespread flooding even reached levels last seen in 2012 after Hurricane Sandy, WFMZ reported.
Neighboring New York was also walloped by rain and wind all day, which caused the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade to be postponed due to the weather for the first time in city history.
The Midwest and the South saw unusual snow for this time of year, with St Louis, Missouri, getting 7.3 inches between Wednesday and Thursday, and snowfall even being spotted in Alabama and Tennessee on Thanksgiving morning.

By Clara Schoenthaler
ROME, Nov 27 (Reuters) - Hunger is set to worsen significantly in 16 global hotspots over the coming six months, with famine threatening parts of Africa, two United Nations agencies warned on Friday.
The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and World Food Programme (WFP) said Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, northern Nigeria and Yemen faced the gravest threats, driven by conflict, displacement, economic hardship and extreme weather.
The number of hunger hotspots has risen from 13 in the previous report released in June, with Chad, Uganda, and parts of both southern Africa and Central America added to the list, while Lebanon was removed.

title: Russia’s upper house ratifies treaty with Zimbabwe on transfer of sentenced persons
summary: In accordance with the treaty, a criminal convicted in one country may be transferred to the other country to serve the sentence
text:
MOSCOW, November 27. /TASS/. The Federation Council, or the upper house of the Russian parliament, ratified the Treaty between Russia and Zimbabwe on the Transfer of Sentenced Persons at a plenary meeting on Friday.
The bill to ratify the document was earlier submitted to the State Duma by Russian President Vladimir Putin. The treaty itself was signed in Moscow and Harare on May 18. As part of agreements, Russia and Zimbabwe will provide each other with the broadest possible assistance in transferring individuals sentenced to imprisonment.
Thus, a criminal convicted in one country may be transferred to the other country to serve the sentence. At that, following a transfer, a convicted person may not be prosecuted or re-convicted for the offenses for which they were originally sentenced.

TAIPEI: Taiwan is set to hold local elections on Saturday (Nov 28) in a closely watched contest seen as a key test of support for the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and the opposition Kuomintang (KMT).
Nearly 20 million voters are eligible to elect 11,051 officials at various levels of government.
This includes city mayors, county magistrates, city and county councillors, as well as lower-level officials such as borough chiefs.
The KMT currently governs 14 of Taiwan's 22 cities and counties, while the DPP controls five.
Some analysts expect the DPP to improve on its performance four years ago, with campaigning largely focused on bread-and-butter issues such as transport and quality-of-life concerns rather than cross-strait relations with China.

title: Conflicts, El Nino worsening hunger: UN food agencies
summary: Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, northern Nigeria and Yemen are the areas of highest concern.
text:
Conflicts, El Nino worsening hunger: UN food agencies
ROME – UN food agencies warned on Nov 27 of worsening hunger over the next six months in 16 mostly African areas, with ongoing conflicts exacerbating already dire conditions in countries like Sudan and Yemen.
While armed conflict and violence are the main reasons for acute food insecurity around the globe, dramatic climate events, including El Nino, are another driver, the joint report from the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) and the World Food Programme (WFP) said.
The Rome-based agencies listed Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, northern Nigeria and Yemen as the areas of highest concern in its early warning about 16 “hunger hot spots” from December until May 2027.
Famine remains a “plausible” risk in parts of Sudan – including North Darfur – and South Sudan, the report found.

Guinea-Bissau's military leaders delay return to civilian rule until 2028
- Published
Guinea-Bissau's military rulers have postponed elections scheduled for next week by two years, delaying the return to civilian rule.
Transitional President Gen Horta N'Tam announced in a decree that the presidential and parliamentary elections, originally due on 6 December, would now take place on 26 November 2028.
The announcement came exactly a year after the military seized power, promising to return the country to civilian rule within 12 months.
In a statement, the presidency said an assessment of electoral preparations had found that there were insufficient "technical, material and financial conditions" to hold the polls as planned.
It said the delay would provide more time to ensure the elections were credible, transparent and inclusive, with all candidates given equal opportunities.

Abdullahi Ibrahim still carries a gun. But he now holds it with one hand.
His left hand was amputated after he sustained a gunshot injury in 2024 while defending his village, Gima, in Anka Local Government Area (LGA) of Zamfara State.
Sitting on a wooden bench and hardly making any effort to conceal the worries that seemed to weigh on him, Mr Ibrahim said that in 2020, bandit attacks became incessant, and he became worried about the recurring attacks on Gima, his village.
In the same year, the armed men stormed his community and kidnapped two people. One of them, who was pregnant, was later released, while the other regained her freedom after a ransom of ₦1 million was paid. But as the attacks continued, local volunteers like Mr Ibrahim took up arms to defend their communities.
Like many, Mr Ibrahim understood the risks of joining a vigilante group to protect his community. But he probably never imagined that a single encounter with the attackers would cost him one of his hands.

Ten years after Rodrigo Duterte launched his deadly crackdown on drugs, thousands of Filipino families are still seeking justice. As the former president prepares to face trial at the ICC, CNA examines the human cost of his campaign, his enduring political influence and the divisions that continue to shape the Philippines.
MANILA / THE HAGUE: At De La Salle University in Manila, a brightly painted van stands out on campus.
The words “Stop the killings” are emblazoned across its side. A mural depicts a woman cradling her dead family. Between windows, a huge “X” crosses over a skull and the words “death squad”.
Above the windscreen is a simple message: “Coffee. Stories. Human rights.”
This is no ordinary coffee van.
It is run by Silingan Coffee, a social enterprise that offers employment to families who lost loved ones during former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte's bloody war on drugs.

text:
Iranian lorry drivers have entered a sixth day of strike action, with protests over the higher cost of living now spreading to 20 cities across the country, the national Union of Truck Drivers' Associations said.
In a statement issued through its Telegram channel on Friday, the union said drivers remain determined to strike due to increasing economic pressure, citing the depreciation of the Iranian rial and the rising cost of conducting business. “Six days have passed, we've reached 20 cities, our voice has reached every corner of Iran … and we are still standing,” the union added.
Drivers are demanding freight rates that reflect the increasing cost of basic industry essential, such as tyres, engine oil and diesel. “Tyres are priced in dollars, oil is priced in dollars, diesel is priced in dollars … freight rates must therefore become realistic,” the union said.

Thousands of women and girls have reported bleeding and miscarriages after French police used tear gas on them during protests.
Cops fired around 22,000 tear gas grenades at protesters on October 17, during the height of the nationwide protests that have rocked France.
Now, activists and health experts fear tens of thousands of women have suffered long-term damage to their reproductive health from being exposed to the tear gas.
Lacrymos de Sang, a feminist collective founded to investigate the possible reproductive effects of tear gas, gathered the testimonies of more than 9,200 women and girls, including school students, who reported exposure to tear gas.
Of those, 94 per cent reported gynaecological symptoms, according to the collective.

One in eight children is stunted. Many have bones that have not matured the way they should. And treatment is hard to find – and harder to afford.
Khan Younis, Gaza – Every time seven-year-old Nabigha al-Zaqzouq stands beside children her age, she notices the difference in their heights and asks her mother, Alia: “Will I ever get taller?”
Nabigha is 99cm (3.2ft) tall and weighs just 10kg (22lb), making her appear several years younger than she actually is.
At home, the family’s dining table reflects part of her struggle. Bread and canned food are among the few options available, while meat, fruit and vegetables are beyond the family’s means. text:
Kobe – The Kobe Municipal Government on Friday submitted to the city assembly a draft ordinance to introduce a tax on vacant condominium units in central areas, aiming to reduce investment-driven vacancies and promote the effective use of housing.
If enacted, it would mark the first tax in Japan targeting vacant condominium units specifically. The city aims to introduce the tax in fiscal 2030.
The levy would be imposed on owners of units without resident registration in condominiums located in such central areas as the Sannomiya and Motomachi districts.
The tax would consist of 0.7% of a condominium unit’s assessed value plus an additional amount based on its location and floor area.
It would be collected as a non-statutory ordinary tax, whose revenue use is not restricted. title: UAE issues first dirham denominated digital sovereign treasury bonds
text:
The UAE has issued its first dirham-denominated digital treasury bonds (digital T-bonds), valued at Dh180 million ($49 million), as part of efforts to develop the domestic debt market, the Ministry of Finance said.
Digital T-bonds refer to government debt that is represented on a blockchain or distributed ledger technology. They use digital tokens and shared ledgers for issuance, trading and settlement.
The ministry used digital infrastructure for the issuance and settlement of bonds, while maintaining integration with traditional settlement and distribution systems, it said on Friday.
The issuance was done through Euroclear’s Digital Financial Market Infrastructure and listed on Nasdaq Dubai.
The digital T-bonds have a two-year tenor and an annual yield to maturity of 4.98 per cent.
It was carried out under the ministry's sovereign treasury bonds programme.

title: Suzuki to domestically produce rare metal-free EV batteries
summary: By making rare metal-free batteries, the company aims to curb procurement risks for materials for which Japan relies on imports.
text:
Suzuki Motor plans to launch the domestic production of lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, batteries, which do not rely on rare metals, for electric vehicles.
Production will start in October 2029, the company said Thursday.
By making rare metal-free batteries, Suzuki aims to curb procurement risks for materials for which Japan relies on imports. “We will build supply chains that do not depend on specific countries,” a company official said.
LFP batteries use iron and phosphorus, and they are thought to be cheaper and safer than what are known as ternary batteries, which depend on rare metals such as nickel, manganese and cobalt.
Suzuki will produce LFP batteries in Japan for the first time. They may also be used as storage batteries in houses.
The company will work with Eliiy Power, a Tokyo-based battery manufacturer, to develop technology for energy-efficient, safe LFP batteries.

title: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
summary: More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia has not.
text:
Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
- Published
Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a new study.
More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.
The only South Asian country where rape within marriage attracts the same penalty as any other rape is The Maldives.
Nepal and Bhutan have criminalised marital rape, but apply lesser penalties, says the study by Samaj, a coalition of women's rights groups in the region.
South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.

For 10 days, two-month-old Mostafa Hallawin has been bedridden at Al-Rantisi Children’s Hospital in Gaza City.

summary: [Capital FM] Nairobi -- Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa has received a ceremonial 21-gun salute and inspected a guard of honour ahead of bilateral talks with President William Ruto, marking the start of his two-day State Visit to Kenya.
text:
Nairobi — Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa has received a ceremonial 21-gun salute and inspected a guard of honour ahead of bilateral talks with President William Ruto, marking the start of his two-day State Visit to Kenya.
Mnangagwa was accorded the full military honours at State House, Nairobi, where he was formally received by President Ruto during an official welcoming ceremony.

With the arrival of the first severe cold spell in late November, European countries with the largest gas storage capacities set all-time records for daily withdrawals from underground gas storage facilities for this time of year, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
On November 25, record withdrawals for that date were registered in Germany (191 mln cubic meters), France (130 mln cubic meters), Italy (90 mln cubic meters), and Austria (52 mln cubic meters). In the Netherlands, withdrawals were the third-highest on record.

Oil is on track to post its first weekly gain this month as attacks on energy infrastructure in the Middle East and vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz fuel concerns over global crude supplies.
Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world’s oil, was up 0.95 per cent to $97.49 a barrel at 11.30 am UAE time, while West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, was trading 2.98 per cent higher at $86.17 a barrel.

title: A documentarian’s painstaking portrait of Bunyo Ishikawa, the ‘Battlefield Bohemian’
summary: Former NHK director Atsunori Kawamura spent seven years making his documentary about a photojournalist on the front lines.
text:
Dozens of photojournalists died while covering conflicts in Southeast Asia in the 1960s and 1970s, including several Japanese. Two became the subject of films: Kyoichi Sawada (1936-1970) with the 1997 documentary “Sawada: From Aomori to Vietnam” and Taizo Ichinose (1947-1973) with the 1999 biopic “One Step on a Mine, It’s All Over.”
Now, former NHK director Atsunori Kawamura has made “Battlefield Bohemian: Photojournalist Bunyo Ishikawa,” a documentary about a contemporary of Sawada and Ichinose who survived to tell his own tale.
“(Ishikawa’s) unique perspective was really appealing to me as a director,” Kawamura tells The Japan Times during an interview at K’s Cinema in Shinjuku, where the film opens on Nov. 28.

SEOUL, Nov. 27 (Yonhap) -- Prosecutors on Friday asked an appellate court to dismiss appeals filed by five key figures in a development corruption scandal linked to President Lee Jae Myung, who were sentenced to prison terms last year.
Prosecutors made the request during a hearing at the Seoul High Court, where the five defendants stood trial over their roles in the Daejang-dong development scandal that occurred in Seongnam, just south of Seoul, in 2015, when Lee was the city's mayor.
The scandal centers on allegations that a small number of obscure private asset management firms, including Hwacheon Daeyu, were allowed to reap astronomical profits from the project.
In October last year, the Seoul Central District Court sentenced Yoo Dong-gyu, former acting president of Seongnam Development Corp., and Kim Man-bae, major shareholder of Hwacheon Daeyu, to eight years in prison each on charges including breach of duty.

title: S. Korean won strengthens against U.S. dollar on foreign inflows
summary: SEOUL, Nov. 27 (Yonhap) -- The South Korean won strengthened against the U.S. do...
text:
S. Korean won strengthens against U.S. dollar on foreign inflows
SEOUL, Nov. 27 (Yonhap) -- The South Korean won strengthened against the U.S. dollar Friday, as foreign investors turned net buyers of local stocks.
The won was quoted at 1,337.9 won per dollar at 3:30 p.m., up 4.8 won from the close of the previous stock trading session. It marked the strongest level since last Friday.
The won's advance came as the Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) jumped on expectations of policy support amid volatility in stock markets, likely including the use of a stock market stabilization fund.
Authorities will hold a meeting with heads of major financial firms next Monday to discuss ways to cope with instability in the market.
 Foreign investors bought a net 1.13 trillion won (US$845 million) worth of local shares during the latest regular stock trading session, with the KOSPI surging 4.34 percent to close at 4,915.68.
(END)

title: Number of students not attending school in Japan reaches record
summary: Over half of the students cited in the education ministry's annual report on student issues did not attend school for at least 90 days.
text:
Truancy has continued to rise among elementary and junior high school students in Japan, with a record 359,424 students not attending school fully in fiscal 2025, according to the education ministry’s annual report on student issues.
The ministry counted in its report for fiscal 2025, which ran through March 2026, students who missed at least 30 school days during the school year without a stated cause, such as illness or financial issues. Over half of the students did not attend school for at least 90 separate days, including over 10,000 who did not attend a single day.
The overall figure, which includes those at special needs schools, was up 1.1% from the previous year, marking the 13th consecutive year with an increase. However, the rate of the rise shrank significantly compared to the COVID-19 pandemic years, when the number of such students increased by as much as almost 25% at one period. summary: Europe entered the heating season with record-low gas reserves
text:
MOSCOW, November 27. /TASS/. With the arrival of the first severe cold spell in late November, Europe has returned to record daily gas withdrawals from underground gas storage facilities, having already used more than 10 bln cubic meters of its reserves, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
Europe entered the heating season with record-low gas reserves. More than four weeks have passed since underground gas storage levels peaked in the fall (74.96%), with cumulative withdrawals exceeding the average for the previous five years by 32%. Since the heating season began on October 28, Europe has withdrawn more than 10 bln cubic meters of gas from storage facilities.

Seoul shares rally over 4 pct on hopes of policy support
SEOUL, Nov. 27 (Yonhap) -- South Korean shares ended higher Friday, extending their gains after a volatile week, led by technology shares amid hopes for market-stabilizing measures. The Korean won was trading higher against the U.S. dollar.
After opening 0.37 percent higher, the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) extended its earlier gains to add 204.47 points, or 4.34 percent, to close at 4,915.68.
Last week, financial authorities unveiled a set of measures to address stock market volatility, including raising the limit on share buybacks by listed companies.
 Investors are watching whether the tech rally has staying power after days of volatility driven by doubts over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

summary: The MOEX and RTS indices rose by 0.31% each to 2,343.88 and 899.07 points, respectively
text:
MOSCOW, November 27. /TASS/. The Russian stock market reversed its gains after rising at the opening of the main trading session on the Moscow Exchange, according to trading data. The yuan is strengthening.
The MOEX and RTS indices rose by 0.31% each to 2,343.88 and 899.07 points, respectively, at the opening of the main trading session, according to trading data as of 9:00 a.m. Moscow time. The yuan rose by 5.7 kopecks against the ruble from the previous session’s closing level to 12.341 rubles at the opening of trading on the Moscow Exchange.
By 9:15 a.m. Moscow time, the MOEX Index had reversed its gains, trading at 2,335.7 points (-0.04%), while the RTS Index stood at 895.93 points (-0.04%). Meanwhile, the yuan was up at 12.331 rubles (+4.65 kopecks).

The elder Talbott was educated at Yale and Oxford, where he bunked with Clinton. Talbott did, and it gave him some notoriety as a young man and a job at the magazine.

12 million girls still marry before the age of 18 every year
27 November 2026
While the first UN International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage and Unions brings much needed recognition of this harmful practice, awareness is not enough. Governments worldwide need to enforce existing laws, invest in girls' education and tackle the root causes of child marriage so all girls can decide their futures.
Plan International has welcomed the establishment of the first UN International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage and Unions (CEFMU), to be marked on 27 November, but warns that international recognition must translate into urgent action.
With 12 million girls still married before the age of 18 every year, Plan is calling on governments worldwide to strengthen protections, enforce existing laws and invest in solutions that enable girls to decide their own futures.

text:
The Supreme Court rules on Friday (November 27, 2026) on one of Canada's most closely watched cases -- a Quebec law barring some provincial employees from wearing religious symbols.
The law has been the subject of intense legal debate since it was first passed by Quebec's government in 2019.
That is partly due to the implications for Quebec, a majority French-speaking province where the decades-long battle to enforce secularism is a core issue and where the Catholic Church once wielded enormous influence over public life.
The case reflects a conflict playing out elsewhere in the world as strictly secular states such as that of France face pressure typical of the Anglo-Saxon world for people to be able to practice their religion freely, including wearing whatever symbols of it that they wish.
The Quebec case is also seen as a major test of how far provinces can go in defying provisions of the federal constitution by invoking the so-called "notwithstanding clause."

Paris-based international news agency Agence France-Presse (AFP) has taken its AFP Forum content platform offline after a cyberattack, its management said on Thursday.

"As soon as the intrusion was detected, our teams moved immediately to contain the intrusion and took AFP Forum offline as a precautionary measure. AFP Forum remains unavailable until further notice," the email said.
The agency said it was providing alternative solutions to subscribers while the platform remains inaccessible.
"An investigation is under way with the help of outside experts. At this stage, we have no information on who is behind the attack," the statement added.

title: Erdogan completes Turkey's ratification of Mecca defence pact
summary: ISTANBUL, Nov 27 - President Tayyip Erdogan has formally approved the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, the Official Gazette said on Friday, completing Turkey's ratification after parliament ratified it earlier this month.
text:
Erdogan completes Turkey's ratification of Mecca defence pact
ISTANBUL, Nov 27 - President Tayyip Erdogan has formally approved the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, the Official Gazette said on Friday, completing Turkey's ratification after parliament ratified it earlier this month.
The three countries signed a joint defence agreement in Mecca in August amid escalating concerns about the increasingly aggressive US-Israeli war against Iran and they are scheduled to hold a meeting in Islamabad on Friday and Saturday.
Turkey's parliament ratified the agreement on November 5, clearing the way for Ankara to send military support to Riyadh amid attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants against the kingdom. Under the agreement, an attack on one party constitutes an attack on all.
A ruling party lawmaker told Reuters last month that Turkey would also submit to parliament a mandate allowing for military personnel to be deployed to Saudi Arabia under the pact.

text:
Moody’s Keeps Eswatini Rating, Warns on Debt
A credit rating is a grade for how safely a government repays its debts. Eswatini keeps its grade, but the agency has raised its debt forecast.
Moody’s Ratings, the US credit rating agency, has affirmed Eswatini’s sovereign rating at B2 with a stable outlook, in a recent rating action. B2 sits below investment grade, the category for borrowers that carry a higher risk of default.
It is the grade Moody’s gave in November 2024 when it lifted the small southern African kingdom from B3. What has changed is the debt forecast: Moody’s now expects government debt to settle at 50% to 52% of GDP (gross domestic product, the size of the economy) over 2026 to 2028, higher than it projected at the upgrade.

title: Europa League match suspended after Georgian police clash with Besiktas fans over Palestinian flag
text:
Thursday's Europa League match between Besiktas and Hapoel Beer-Sheva was suspended for 30 minutes after Georgian police clashed with Turkish fans after they unfurled a Palestinian flag.
Referee Morten Krogh halted proceedings in the 26th minute after disturbances broke out among the travelling Turkish supporters, with footage showing police confronting Besiktas fans and one spectator being carried out of the stadium on a stretcher.

KARACHI: For residents of Karachi Administration Cooperative Housing Society, the rubble of the six-storey collapsed building represents far more than a violation of the city’s building regulations. They believe the tragedy reflects a wider construction system in which the builder mafia, the indifference of relevant authorities and the misuse of official powers have put human lives at risk.
They added that the collapse had once again exposed how the rule of law and institutional accountability in the city had been reduced to little more than official claims.
According to them, after every tragedy, officials arrive at the scene, issue statements shifting responsibility onto one another and announce investigations. With the passage of time, however, public attention fades, while the question of who should be held responsible remains unanswered.
One resident, expressing anger over the incident, asked how a building approved for ground-plus-one construction could have reached six storeys.

title: Earth exceeds 2C of warming for seven consecutive days for the first time
summary: The planet's average temperature exceeded pre-industrial levels by more than 2C for seven consecutive days, something that had never happened before, the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the European Earth observation programme, has confirmed. On Monday, November 23, the largest daily anomaly ever measured was also recorded: 2.25C above the 1850-1900 period.
text:
The planet's average temperature exceeded pre-industrial levels by more than 2C for seven consecutive days, something that had never happened before, the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the European Earth observation programme, has confirmed. On Monday, November 23, the largest daily anomaly ever measured was also recorded: 2.25C above the 1850-1900 period.
The 2C threshold was reached on ten days in November — the 3rd, 4th, 13th and from the 18th to the 24th — seven of them consecutively. On November 23, the global average temperature was also 1.34C above the 1991-2020 average. These are not the highest absolute temperatures, which usually occur in July and August, but the largest deviation from normal for this time of year. Until now, 2C had been exceeded on only two days in November 2023 and four in February 2024. The data are preliminary, although Copernicus does not expect changes of more than 0.02C.

title: Look up! The low-altitude economy is taking off
text:
A new economy is forming in the sky above us. Drones carry medicines, inspect power lines, treat crops and deliver parcels; passenger services will soon follow. This is the low-altitude economy, a new economy that uses air space mostly below 1,000 metres, sometimes up to 3,000. Its actors are all machines and robots that range from helicopters and drones to electric vertical take-off and landing craft, or eVTOLs. Cheaper sensors, electric motors and better software are making routine flights practical – and creating new jobs, and a whole new economy in aviation, data, maintenance and logistics.
In western Sweden, emergency despatchers send drones carrying automated external defibrillators when an ambulance is alerted to suspected cardiac arrest. In a study of 55 cases, drones arrived first in 37, with a median lead of three minutes and 14 seconds. In cardiac arrest cases, seconds can mean the difference between life and death, and the drone puts equipment on scene before paramedics.

Tokyo Electric Power Company Holdings said Thursday it would review its plan to complete by August 2029 an anti-terrorism facility for the No. 7 reactor at its Kashiwazaki-Kariwa nuclear power plant in Niigata Prefecture.
The contracting company has informed Tepco that construction needs to be extended by more than a year because of factors including labor shortages, the power supplier said.
The development is expected to further delay the restart of the reactor after Tepco previously pushed back the facility’s completion from October 2025. No revised completion target has been set.
An anti-terrorism facility has also yet to be completed for the plant’s No. 6 reactor, which was restarted in January this year. The reactor will be unable to continue operating unless the facility is finished by April 2031.

title: AI unleashes a new era of cybersecurity
summary: A shortage of cybersecurity professionals remains one of the biggest barriers to resilience.
text:
While there have been concerns about the safety and security of cyberspace since it was invented, the last few months have been especially harrowing. There have been high-profile hacks, outages and incidents that hammered home the vulnerabilities that come when societies are threaded together with virtual strings.
Industry experts reckon that the total losses generated by cyberattacks in any given year is in the trillions of dollars; the figure is likely unknowable given the frequency and opacity of many if not most such incidents. The headlines of the last few weeks suggest that we have entered an AI-empowered era in which the scale, scope, speed and frequency of those assaults will be significantly increased.
There is hope, however. The anxiety and recognition that AI creates a fundamentally new era for cybersecurity is the start. If governments, businesses and individuals adopt this new mindset, the damage will be mitigated, though we must be ready for steady-state anxiety.

summary: SEOUL, Nov. 27 (Yonhap) -- South Koreans' overseas card spending hit the highest...
text:
Overseas card spending hits record high in Q3
SEOUL, Nov. 27 (Yonhap) -- South Koreans' overseas card spending hit the highest-ever amount in the third quarter of the year on the back of an increase in outbound travelers, data showed Friday.
The amount of money spent overseas by South Koreans with credit and debit cards came to US$6.63 billion in the July-September period, up 13.3 percent from three months earlier, according to data from the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The on-quarter rise marks the sharpest since the first quarter of 2023, when the reading spiked 14.8 percent, and also is the largest-ever.
The central bank said more South Koreans traveled overseas, although direct purchases from abroad declined.
The number of overseas travelers came to 7.12 million in the third quarter of the year, up 7.4 percent from the previous quarter.
 The combined amount of purchases made through overseas shopping malls, on the other hand, fell 0.8 percent to $1.4 billion.

text:
OVERVIEW. The outbreak in northwest Mauritania developed in November, with hopper groups and bands southeast of Akjoujt and hopper groups in northern Trarza. Fledging continued, forming more immature groups, some of which started to mature. Breeding started in Western Sahara, where hatching occurred and adult groups were laying. Survey and control operations must continue. Isolated adults were also reported in Algeria, Niger and Egypt; none in India.
WHY IT MATTERS. With recent rains in northwest Mauritania, new adult groups could mature and lay eggs, producing a new generation of hopper groups and bands from late December; breeding in Western Sahara will also produce more hopper groups. More adults may appear in northern Mauritania. If left uncontrolled, this could lead to more adult groups and small swarms in the coming months.

summary: The changes come as the nursing care insurance system faces funding and other challenges amid growing demand for nursing care services.
text:
The health ministry is considering raising nursing care insurance premiums for some older people with an annual income of ¥1.2 million ($7,500) or more after public pension and other deductions, effective from fiscal 2027, which begins in April, sources said Thursday.
The ministry also plans to implement measures to reduce the premium burden on low-income earners, according to its premium review plans presented at the day’s meeting of the Social Security Council.
The changes come as the nursing care insurance system faces funding and other challenges amid growing demand for nursing care services in Japan’s graying society.
The system collects premiums from people who are 65 and older. Municipal governments set standard premium amounts, and the nationwide average is ¥6,225 per month for the period between fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2026. Standard premium amounts are reviewed once every three years.

title: Faster inflation in Tokyo supports case for BOJ rate hike in December
summary: The consumer price index excluding fresh food rose 2.9% in November from a year earlier in the capital, the highest level since July 2025, data shows.
text:
Inflation in Tokyo has accelerated to its fastest pace this year, backing the case for a rate increase by the Bank of Japan next month as authorities focus on keeping price growth around their 2% target.
The consumer price index (CPI) excluding fresh food rose 2.9% in November from a year earlier in Tokyo, the highest level since July 2025, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications reported Friday. The result matched the consensus forecast of economists.
Tokyo inflation is a leading indicator of nationwide price trends. The index that strips out both fresh food and energy, a gauge closely monitored by the BOJ as a measure of underlying inflation, climbed 2.5%, while overall CPI rose 2.8%.
